destination.name: Western Ukraine
destination.label: Western Ukraine — home base, where the cards land

participants.name: Angela (& rep)
participants.bio: A child of Oshawa's Ukrainian community, Angela protests outside the russian embassy in Ottawa several times a week. She draws her own postcards — tryzubs, flags and hearts — and each month gathers the protesters for postcard-writing cafés: a few hundred original cards and counting.
participants.pullQuote: Don't think about what you can't do – focus on what you can do.
participants.quoteContext: Her monthly postcard cafés with the embassy protesters have produced hundreds of original designs. Drawing tryzubs, flags and hearts, she says, is how she processes fear of the war news without burning out.

publicAttrs.ukraineTie: child of the Oshawa Ukrainian community
publicAttrs.rallies: the russian embassy in Ottawa, several times a week

participants.name: Helen

media.title: Get to know the Team … An Interview with Helen

participants.bio: Helen launched the Canada branch from Millbrook, Ontario, with Jean-Michel, after years teaching in a Ukrainian democracy-education project. She draws Zentangle patterns, and every card sent through Canada passes through her hands on its way to the front.
participants.pullQuote: Nobody was dropping bombs on my house, so the least I could do was launch a Canadian branch.
participants.quoteContext: On the day of the invasion, she and Jean-Michel decided to act; a Postcrossing message from Peter in Australia showed the way. With guidance from Tamara in Ukraine, the Canada branch was rolling within a week.

participants.name: Kamloops Stands with Ukraine
participants.bio: Kamloops Stands with Ukraine group has gathered to stand in solidarity with Ukraine every Saturday since the invasion — snow, rain, or scorching heat.
participants.pullQuote: The living proof that postcards heal, one moment at a time.
participants.quoteContext: Rose in Oshawa forwarded the newsletters; Michelle made card-writing central to the Kamloops rallies, helping newcomers attempt their first Ukrainian phrases in Cyrillic. Co-founder Sasha Krasun teaches the group's online Stand with Ukraine class and wrote “Postcards That Carry Courage” about how the project reached them.

participants.name: Kerry

media.title: A Little Comfort from Australia: Adaptive T-Shirts for Ukraine’s Injured Defenders

links.title: A Little Comfort from Australia: Adaptive T-Shirts for Ukraine’s Injured Defenders
Introducing Australia branch's social media manager, Kerry

participants.bio: Kerry, a technology and sewing teacher in Victoria originally from the UK, turned her school into a card-writing engine: 110 students' cards in one round, a Ukrainian flag over the yard, a quilt block to wrap a war-torn building in love. Now she adapts T-shirts for injured Defenders, sending them with postcards to Vinnytsia.
participants.pullQuote: Seeing the photos of Defenders proudly holding cards and hearing their joy at reading a card … How could you not think it worthwhile?
participants.quoteContext: She met the project at Geelong's Mama's Market in 2023 and now runs PTTF Australia's social media. A Defender she corresponds with receives her students' translated messages.

participants.name: Nadia
participants.bio: Nadia quit her pharmacist's job when the rockets came, then returned to work — one way to normalize an unnormal life. A relative defends Ukraine; they message every day and have met twice in two years.
participants.pullQuote: I realized that the world is not indifferent to what is happening in Ukraine. And this support gave me strength and courage not to give up and move on.
participants.quoteContext: Postcrossing brought her the world's support after 2022. The project, she says, made an incredible impression — it unites so many people in different parts of the world.

participants.name: Tamara

links.title: Life During the War: A Personal Story from Tamara

participants.bio: Tamara, a Postcrosser, coordinates Postcards to the Front from Ukraine, where your cards finally land. She left her beloved Zaporizhzhia for the safer west — boyfriend, bandura and Mr. Cat in tow — and hands the cards to the Defenders who ask for them by the hundreds.
participants.pullQuote: My energy often runs out before my gratitude does.
participants.quoteContext: The founder's honest account: leaving home meant choosing safety over comfort, a small van packed with everything. Your postcards, she says, mean the world — even on the days the blackouts win.

participants.name: Voice of Ukraine

media.title: Voice of Ukraine – rallies to support Ukraine in beautiful British Columbia

participants.bio: Voices of Ukraine stands up for Ukraine in public across British Columbia — rallying every Sunday at Vancouver’s Canada Place, and in Coquitlam — and its supporters write postcards to the Defenders they rally for.
participants.pullQuote: Even a few kind words can lift someone’s spirit on a hard day. It’s such a simple gesture that shows our humanity and solidarity.
participants.quoteContext: Liliia rallies at Canada Place every Sunday; Olena gathers Coquitlam’s Ukrainian families. Six B.C. branches raise funds for medical aid — and write postcards to the Defenders they stand for.

participants.name: Judy R.

media.title: Writing postcards may lift someone up

participants.bio: A former nurse and substitute teacher, Judy has joined the protests outside the russian embassy in Ottawa whenever she is in town since March 2022 — through scorching sun and freezing sleet. She makes collage postcards from magazines and junk mail.
participants.pullQuote: Writing postcards feels, in a minuscule way, like I may be able to lift someone up, if even for a moment.
participants.quoteContext: A fellow embassy protester, Karen, introduced her to the project. Judy builds collage postcards from magazines and junk mail, and asks fellow protesters Angela and Nadia to translate her Ukrainian phrases.

publicAttrs.rallies: the russian embassy in Ottawa, since March 2022

participants.name: Roland

media.title: One small step from Australia toward a European vision

participants.bio: Roland attends and speaks at public rallies for Ukraine in Darmstadt, where people have rallied against the war every week — more than 200 times. Before that he fought russian disinformation online. His first postcard event sent 54 cards to a brigade at the front.
participants.pullQuote: If it really doesn't exist, I thought, let's make it happen.
participants.quoteContext: His brother photographed a Postcards to the Front poster at Ukifest in Sydney. Finding nothing like it in Germany or the EU, Roland started in Darmstadt — Uzhhorod's sister city since 1992 — hoping the idea spreads across Europe.

publicAttrs.foundVia: his brother's photo from a festival in Sydney

participants.name: Isis

media.title: Sending postcards to Defenders more important than I realized

participants.bio: Isis paints her postcards in watercolour on her family's farm in rural Ontario — chickens, horses, flamingos, fields and forests, each with the colours of Ukraine's flag somewhere on it. Learning watercolour is part of her recovery from a serious health issue.
participants.pullQuote: While I can't go to public events, creating these postcards and sending my support is something that I can do.
participants.quoteContext: She found the project on social media. Her hand-painted cards won a prize in the 2026 Ukrainian Heritage Month challenge, and she adds a few words in Ukrainian to each one.

participants.name: Duncan

media.title: Postcards provide some small but meaningful support

participants.bio: Duncan is a nurse in Australia who writes to Ukraine's Defenders every month. A keen student of history since his teens, he believes empires never rise again — and that Ukraine, as a sovereign state, has every right to choose its own alliances.
participants.pullQuote: We must do all that we can to support the defence of their homeland.
participants.quoteContext: His other passions are electronics and cycling, and he is fluent in German. He hopes the war ends soon, and with it the suffering of Ukrainians and Russians alike.

participants.name: Corinne
participants.bio: Corinne rallies residents of Macleay Island, off the Queensland coast, to write to Ukraine: a community of 4,000 that has sent 3,000 postcards in four years, including cards hand-painted by the island's primary school children.
participants.quoteContext: She adopted Crackles, one of six lake ducks residents saved when the council wanted them gone. Crackles came with an injured foot; now she models outfits in Ukrainian colours and appears on the island's cards.

participants.name: Peter (Goulburn)

media.title: For a soldier, any mail is a morale booster

participants.bio: A retired lawyer in Goulburn, Peter spent two decades as a soldier and remembers what mail meant far from home. He writes his postcards in Ukrainian, and in 2023 travelled to Kyiv and Odesa to study the language.
participants.pullQuote: I will continue writing Postcards to the Front for as long as the need is there.
participants.quoteContext: His youngest granddaughter calls a good day at school ‘a Ukrainian day’ and a bad one ‘a Russian day’. A Ukrainian flag rides on the side of his car.

publicAttrs.ukraineTie: travelled to Kyiv and Odesa to study Ukrainian

participants.name: Valentin

media.title: A Call for Model Railroad Magazines

participants.bio: Valentin is a Ukrainian Postcrosser who loves stamps, the history of mail and model railways — his H0-scale layout is called Rheintal, Linie 87. Helen has sent him postcards for nearly five years; this October his Maine Coon, Mavka, had five kittens.
participants.pullQuote: In times like these, everyone really needs some kind of outlet, a hobby to switch off from the harsh reality.
participants.quoteContext: He asked readers for back issues of Model Railroader or the Australian Model Railway Magazine to read on long winter evenings, and Helen put out the call in the newsletter.

participants.name: Anna M.

media.title: Zolota Ptakha: a Ukrainian postcard brand born from a love of Postcrossing

participants.bio: Anna founded Zolota Ptakha, a Kyiv postcard brand, in ninth grade — after her mother introduced her to Postcrossing to practise her English. Today she is its creative director and an illustrator who draws as AnniKa, keeping the brand running through air raids and power cuts.
participants.pullQuote: Knowing that our postcards continue to travel around the world and bring joy to others gives us the strength to keep creating.
participants.quoteContext: Zolota Ptakha supplied the prizes for the project's 2026 Ukrainian Heritage Month challenge. Anna also illustrates as AnniKa, and the brand prints on recycled paper.
